q-170669.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{2y-x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{2y-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=e2y−x,x=cos⁡t and y=sin⁡t, compute dfdt.

a
(sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
b
e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
c
(2sin⁡tcos⁡t+1)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
d
(2sin⁡t−cos⁡t)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
e
2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−e2y−x,∂f∂y=2e2y−x

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t,∂f∂y=2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=−sin⁡t,dydt=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=(sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

q-95080.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
s(s+2)es2+2s
b
2(s+2)es2+2s
c
2ses2+2s
d
2(s+1)es2+2s
e
s2es2+2s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ex+2y,∂f∂y=2ex+2y

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=es2+2s,∂f∂y=2es2+2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=es2+2s⋅2s+2es2+2s⋅1=2ses2+2s+2es2+2s=2(s+1)es2+2s.

q-95078.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡t-\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2),x=cos⁡t and y=sin⁡t, compute dfdt for 0<t<π2.

a
2csc⁡t−tan⁡t
b
sec⁡t−tan⁡t
c
2tan⁡t−cot⁡t
d
cot⁡t+2csc⁡t
e
2cot⁡t−tan⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=y2xy2=1x,∂f∂y=2xyxy2=2y

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=1cos⁡t,∂f∂y=2sin⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=−sin⁡t,dydt=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=1cos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tcos⁡t+2⋅cos⁡tsin⁡t=2cot⁡t−tan⁡t.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot 1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}+{t}^{2}\cdot t{e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}={e}^{{t}^{3}}+{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{3}}=(1+{t}^{3}){e}^{{t}^{3}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =({t}^{2})^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}={t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =(1+{t}^{3}){e}^{{t}^{3}}\cdot 2t+{t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1 \\  & =(2t+2{t}^{4}){e}^{{t}^{3}}+{t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}} \\  & =(2t+3{t}^{4}){e}^{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=xexy,x=t2, and y=t, compute dfdt.

a
(2+t2)et3
b
(3t+2t3)et2
c
(2t+3t4)et3
d
(2+3t3)et2
e
(3t+2t4)et3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=exy+xyexy,∂f∂y=x2exy

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=et2⋅t+t2⋅tet2⋅t=et3+t3et3=(1+t3)et3,∂f∂y=(t2)2et2⋅t=t4et3.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2t,dydt=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=(1+t3)et3⋅2t+t4et3⋅1=(2t+2t4)et3+t4et3=(2t+3t4)et3.

q-170670.name: Question 6
q-170670.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95114.html:
Question 8
?

If f(x,y)=x2+y2 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
1+3x41+x4
b
3x41+x4
c
1+3x3x1+x4
d
1+x21+x4
e
3x21+x4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=xx2+y2,∂f∂y=yx2+y2

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=xx2+x6=xx2(1+x4)=xx1+x4=11+x4,∂f∂y=x3x2+x6=x3x2(1+x4)=x3x1+x4=x21+x4.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=3x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=11+x4+x21+x4⋅3x2=11+x4+3x41+x4=1+3x41+x4.

q-94752.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =({e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t})(s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+({e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t})(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(s\operatorname{cos}⁡t-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t){e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =s(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t){e}^{s(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
s(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
b
(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)

(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)

s(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=ex+y,∂f∂y=ex+y

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=essin⁡t+scos⁡t,∂f∂y=essin⁡t+scos⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=scos⁡t,∂y∂t=−ssin⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=(essin⁡t+scos⁡t)(scos⁡t)+(essin⁡t+scos⁡t)(−ssin⁡t)=(scos⁡t−ssin⁡t)essin⁡t+scos⁡t=s(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t).

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =1, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(-1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Let f(x,y)=x−y, where x=−scos⁡t and y=ssin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
−(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)
b
cos⁡t−sin⁡t
c
2cos⁡t
d
s(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
e
s(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=1,∂f∂y=−1

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=1,∂f∂y=−1.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=−cos⁡t,∂y∂s=sin⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(1)(−cos⁡t)+(−1)(sin⁡t)=−(cos⁡t+sin⁡t).

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y)=xy, where x=cos⁡t+sin⁡s and y=sin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
1+sin⁡ssin⁡t
b
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡scos⁡t
c
1+cos⁡scos⁡t
d
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t
e
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡ssin⁡t
Submit

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=sin⁡t,∂f∂y=cos⁡t+sin⁡s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=−sin⁡t,∂y∂t=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=sin⁡t(−sin⁡t)+(cos⁡t+sin⁡s)⋅cos⁡t=−sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t.

$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y)=xy2−2y, where x=st2 and y=s3−t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
7s3t2−4s3t3−6s
b
3s6t2−6s2+t4

Submit

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y2,∂f∂y=2xy−2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=(s3−t)2=s6−2s3t+t2,∂f∂y=2(st2)(s3−t)−2=2s4t2−2st3−2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=t2,∂y∂s=3s2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(s6−2s3t+t2)(t2)+(2s4t2−2st3−2)(3s2)=s6t2−2s3t3+t4+6s6t2−6s3t3−6s2=7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{-s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{-s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{-s} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2xx2+y2,∂f∂y=2yx2+y2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2(tes)(tes)2+(te−s)2=2est(e2s+e−2s),∂f∂y=2(te−s)(tes)2+(te−s)2=2e−st(e2s+e−2s).

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=es,∂y∂t=e−s.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=2est(e2s+e−2s)⋅es+2e−st(e2s+e−2s)⋅e−s=2e2st(e2s+e−2s)+2e−2st(e2s+e−2s)=2(e2s+e−2s)t(e2s+e−2s)=2t.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14271739/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=st,∂f∂y=s2+t2+st2,∂f∂z=st+2st2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=2s,∂y∂s=1t,∂z∂s=t2.

$$

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

Question 18
?

Let f(x,y,z)=xyz, where x=2, y=set and z=tes. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
4(t−s)et+s
b
2s(t+1)et+s
c
2(t+s)et+s
d
4t(s−1)et+s
e
2t(s+1)et+s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=yz,∂f∂y=xz,∂f∂z=xy.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=2tes,∂f∂z=2set.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=0,∂y∂t=set,∂z∂t=es.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(tset+s)⋅0+(2tes)⋅set+(2set)⋅es=2tset+s+2set+s=2s(t+1)et+s.
